chicken-or-turkey-rice-corn-and-cheese-w.title: Chicken or Turkey with Rice, Corn and Cheese in Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of pieces of chicken or turkey, boiled rice, corn kernels and grated cheese, all covered with a savory gravy. It is a common offering in school cafeterias and family meals, providing a balanced mix of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are complete protein sources containing all essential amino acids.
Long-grain rice is usually used, keeping its shape after cooking.
Corn adds a sweet note and boosts the fiber content.
A mild, melt‑friendly cheese is typically chosen to blend smoothly into the gravy.
The gravy is often based on broth and cream, giving the dish a rich, velvety texture.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken or turkey supplies essential proteins needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑rich carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides quick‑release carbs that fuel active days.

items.title: Fiber and vitamins
items.content: Corn contributes dietary fiber, vitamin B6 and antioxidants that support digestion.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: Moderate saturated fat
items.content: Using low‑fat cheese and a modest amount of gravy keeps the dish relatively light.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravies can be salty; those monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Processed meat additives
items.content: If pre‑processed chicken or turkey is used, it may contain preservatives or additives.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage above 4 °C can allow bacterial growth, so keep the dish refrigerated promptly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically in individual portions. It can be enjoyed as a standalone meal or paired with a fresh vegetable salad. Garnish with chopped herbs or a dash of hot sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or on the stovetop, adding a splash of water to prevent the gravy from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Chili Hot Dog, No Bun is a beef sausage coated with a spicy chili sauce made from tomatoes, peppers and seasonings, served without the traditional bun. It is popular among low‑carb and keto diet followers and those looking for a quick, bold flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chili hot dogs without buns are a staple in keto menus as a substitute for regular hot dogs.
The spicy sauce can contain over 10 % capsaicin, the compound responsible for the heat.
In the United States, “bun‑less” versions are often wrapped in mozzarella cheese, but this product uses only meat and spices.
The product is vacuum‑packed, extending shelf life without added preservatives.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Without the bun, the product contains less than 2 g of carbs, making it suitable for keto and low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef sausage supplies a notable amount of heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Spicy sauce may boost metabolism
items.content: Capsaicin in chili can slightly increase metabolic rate and aid calorie burning.

items.title: Spicy food
items.content: Very hot sauce may cause stomach irritation or heartburn in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed meats often contain high levels of salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: If not fresh, nitrites may be added to preserve color; excess intake is undesirable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, wrapped in lettuce leaves, or used as a filling for low‑carb wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. When frozen, it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Instant coffee, reconstituted (5202) is a dry powder made from brewed coffee extract that regains its aroma and flavor when hot water is added. It is convenient, quick to prepare, and retains most of the sensory qualities of regular brewed coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Instant coffee was first produced commercially in the early 20th century.
Two main drying methods are used: spray‑drying and freeze‑drying; the latter preserves more aromatic compounds.
Reconstituted instant coffee often contains stabilizers and antioxidants to extend shelf life.
It is classified by roast level—light, medium, dark—each offering a distinct flavor profile.
In several countries, instant coffee is a staple part of the breakfast routine.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress in the body.

items.title: Supports cognitive function
items.content: Caffeine can improve alertness, memory, and reaction time.

items.title: Boosts metabolism
items.content: Caffeine increases metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: May lower risk of certain diseases
items.content: Regular moderate coffee consumption is linked to reduced risk of type 2 diabetes and some cancers.

items.title: Enhances physical endurance
items.content: Caffeine raises adrenaline levels, which can improve athletic performance.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after coffee.

items.title: Increased stomach acidity
items.content: Coffee can aggravate gastritis or acid reflux in susceptible people.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Certain instant coffees contain artificial flavors or sweeteners that may not suit everyone.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of some medications, especially CNS stimulants.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1‑2 teaspoons of powder to 200‑250 ml of hot (not boiling) water, stir, and let steep for 30 seconds. Adjust with milk, cream, sugar, or sweetener to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a dry, cool place and seal it tightly after each use. Prevent moisture exposure to avoid clumping and flavor loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Coleslaw is a classic salad made from finely shredded cabbage, carrots and sometimes radish, dressed with mayonnaise, vinegar, mustard and spices. It is commonly served as a side dish in fast‑food and quick‑service restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coleslaw originated in New England in the 19th century as a way to preserve cabbage through the winter.
The original recipe used only fermented cabbage, but most modern versions use fresh white cabbage.
There are many variations: with apples, pineapple, cranberries or even avocado.
In the United States coleslaw is a typical side for barbecue; in Japan it appears as “coleslaw rolls” wrapped in nori.
Cabbage retains most of its vitamin C when the salad is not over‑cooked.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Fresh cabbage provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in calories (when lightly dressed)
items.content: With a moderate amount of dressing, coleslaw can be a light side dish with relatively few calories.

items.title: Contains probiotics (in fermented versions)
items.content: Fermented cabbage in coleslaw supplies beneficial bacteria that support gut health.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cabbage and carrots contain carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Mayonnaise allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise can trigger allergic reactions in people sensitive to eggs or mustard.

items.title: High fat content with generous dressing
items.content: A large amount of mayonnaise increases calories and saturated fat.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, bacteria can multiply in the salad.

items.title: Added sugar in some recipes
items.content: Sweetened coleslaw versions may contain added sugar, which is undesirable for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve coleslaw chilled as a side to burgers, fried chicken, fish or barbecue. It can be added to sandwiches, tacos, or used as a filling for wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep coleslaw in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑5 days. For longer storage, keep the dressing separate from the cabbage to maintain crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg Benedict is a classic American dish first served in 1953 at the Benedict's restaurant in New York. It consists of a split English muffin topped with a slice of ham, a poached egg, and hollandaise sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is named after its creator, chef George Benedict.
Many variations exist: smoked salmon (Eggs Benedict with salmon), spinach (Eggs Florentine) or avocado.
Hollandaise sauce is made from egg yolks, butter, and lemon juice and must be whisked constantly to prevent curdling.
Poached eggs are cooked without shells in gently simmering water with a splash of vinegar to help the whites set.
Although traditionally a breakfast or brunch item, it is also featured on upscale restaurant menus.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide complete protein with all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The yolk contains B12, B2, and folate, which are important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains vitamin D and choline
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption, while choline supports brain and liver health.

items.title: Healthy fats in the sauce
items.content: Butter in hollandaise supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: Eggs and butter provide calcium and iron, essential for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites, ranging from mild to severe.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should monitor their intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories due to butter and the muffin, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked poached eggs can harbor salmonella; ensure eggs reach a safe temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Egg Benedict hot, immediately after preparation. Add fresh spinach, tomatoes, or avocado for variety. Ham can be swapped for smoked salmon or a vegetarian alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared hollandaise sauce can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Leftover poached eggs and muffins are best consumed within 24 hours to avoid dryness.

rice-brown-with-vegetables-cheese-and-or.title: Brown Rice with Vegetables and Cheese/Cream Sauce, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice prepared with vegetables and a cheese or cream sauce without added fat is a nutritious dish that combines whole‑grain rice, a variety of vegetables, and a smooth, protein‑rich sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it more nutrient‑dense than white rice.
Typical vegetables include broccoli, carrots, bell peppers, and zucchini, providing a wide range of vitamins and minerals.
The low‑fat cheese or cream sauce is made from fat‑free cottage cheese, yogurt, or plant‑based alternatives, delivering creaminess without extra calories.
The dish is suitable for vegetarians when the sauce uses plant‑based protein sources.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: High in Fiber
items.content: Brown rice supplies soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Source of Complex Carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy release, aiding prolonged activity.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals from Vegetables
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and potassium, essential for immunity and heart function.

items.title: Protein and Calcium from Sauce
items.content: The low‑fat cheese or cream sauce delivers quality protein and calcium for bone health.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: Cheese‑based sauce may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

items.title: Oxalate Content
items.content: Certain vegetables such as spinach are high in oxalates, which should be limited by people prone to kidney stones.

items.title: Sodium Levels
items.content: If the sauce contains added salt, monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main course or as a side to meat, fish, or tofu. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop, and fresh herbs can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it retains quality for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before serving.
